output.methodChoice: EDF v0.3 applied internally. I collected X7 (yield by scholarship tier) and X10 (yield by admission round). Together they separate three rivals: the award-schedule change, the slow regular-decision turnaround, and a general decline in demand.
output.brief: President: the evidence does not support holding Admissions responsible for the enrolment drop. Applications, admits and grades all rose; the loss is in the share of admits who enrolled (41.8% to 34.3%). Nearly all of the 330-student shortfall sits in the two scholarship tiers whose awards were cut last October (Dean's $14,000 to $9,000; Merit $9,000 to $5,000), where the share enrolling fell about 13 points. Presidential scholars (award unchanged) and students without merit awards barely moved. Early-action admits, who got on-time decisions on the old system, fell as much (7.4 points) as regular-decision admits (7.5 points), who waited far longer. So the slow decisions were real and worth fixing, but they don't explain the loss; the award cut most plausibly does. I'm fairly confident (about 80%). Unchecked: competitors' offers, the net-revenue effect, and the missing-transcript complaints. Next: don't replace the director on this basis. Before award letters go out in December, take a proposal to the finance committee restoring awards in the two tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled. Also set a turnaround target, track enrolment rates by segment, and hold off on the vendor rebuild until the transcript issue is checked.
